tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

# AI logs

Evidence for Report Sections 2, 3 and 8: which AI tools we used, what we gave them, and what came back.

## What is captured automatically

Claude Code sessions started inside this repo are copied into `raw/` by the hook in `.claude/hooks/archive_transcript.mjs`. It runs after every turn and when the session ends. `sessions.tsv` lists each session with the git user who ran it.

History of the hook:
- Until 23 October 2026 the hook ran `python3`. On Windows that is a Microsoft Store stub that does nothing, so no transcript was ever archived (audit-1 finding F-01).
- It now runs on `node`, which the project already requires.
- The three sessions that existed by then (Phase 1 setup, Phase 3, audit 1) were archived by running the hook by hand. Their `first_seen_utc` in `sessions.tsv` is therefore the archive time, not the session start.
- The Phase 2 Codex session ran outside Claude Code. No verbatim log of it is held; see `phase2-session.md`.

**Redaction.** The copies in `raw/` are verbatim except for one mechanical rule, applied by the hook: every email address is replaced with `[email-redacted]`. GitHub `@users.noreply.github.com` addresses are left alone, because they are already public in the commit history. This keeps team members' personal and work addresses out of a public repository. It is the only exception to "do not edit transcripts" below. The same rule, with the hook's regular expression, is applied by hand to the readable copies in `exports/` before they are committed. On 4 November 2026 it replaced one address in `exports/2026-10-23-phase3-and-audit-remediation.txt` (line 2635).

**Development keys (decision D10).** The hook also replaces Hardhat's 20 published development private keys with `[hardhat-dev-key-redacted]`, and its default test seed phrase with `[hardhat-dev-mnemonic-redacted]`. These values are public and hold nothing of value, but a public repository should not contain anything that looks like a private key. The hook recognises the keys by their SHA-256 hash, so the hook itself never contains them. Session 069871d2 is the first transcript this applied to: its scan commands had quoted one key and the phrase. Real keys stay in `.env`, which no session reads, so they should never reach a transcript in the first place.

Claude Code only keeps its own transcripts for a limited time, so the copies in `raw/` are the record we rely on. Commit them.

The raw files are JSONL in Claude Code's internal format, which can change between versions. They are the record, not something to read. For the report, use the readable exports below.

## What you do by hand

1. **Name sessions** so they are easy to find: start Claude Code with `claude -n <topic>`, e.g. `claude -n token-contract-gen`.
2. **Export important sessions** before ending them: run `/export docs/ai-logs/exports/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<topic>.txt`. Do this for any session that generated code, changed the spec, or found a bug.
3. **Log other AI tools** (claude.ai chats, ChatGPT, Copilot, Cursor): save or copy the conversation into `exports/` and add a row to `INDEX.md`.
4. **Add an INDEX row** for every session that mattered. Skip trivial ones.

## Rules

- Never paste private keys, RPC URLs with keys, or API keys into any AI tool. These files are committed.
- Do not edit transcripts after the fact. If a session went badly, that is evidence too.

15	| Wallet | Assigned role |

1	# Spec v1: frozen specification
2	
3	Status: FROZEN. No `TODO(decision)` markers remain.
4	
5	Phase 2 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 2 requirements](phase2-requirements.md) govern token implementation where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, AccessControl delegates compliance administration, revoking eligibility preserves existing balances, and pause/freeze/forced transfer are not implemented in this phase. See [implementation decisions](../phase2-implementation.md) for the exact API and scope. The original requirements below remain preserved for audit comparison.
6	
7	Phase 3 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 3 requirements](phase3-requirements.md) govern AssetFactory and AssetSale where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, the function names change (`authorizeIssuer`, `revokeIssuer`, `buyTokens`, `pricePerToken`), the registry gains `getAsset` / `getAssetCount` with description and asset-type metadata, and a sale can be closed so unsold inventory can be recovered. The decisions are recorded in that file. The reentrancy requirement and invariant 8 below still apply.
8	
9	Decision D5 (opened 23 October 2026 in [phase3-requirements.md](phase3-requirements.md); decided 3 November 2026): **pause and forced transfer are implemented; freeze is dropped.** Freeze adds nothing because whitelist revocation already does the same job. Since Phase 2 §2.3, a revoked holder keeps their balance but can neither send, receive nor buy (invariant 1). So "freeze" in this spec now means revoking eligibility with `setWhitelisted(addr, false)`. The governing function rows are in §5 under "D5 functions", and invariants 1, 5, 6 and 7 are restated. Everywhere else, a mention of freeze (§1 "Why a blockchain", the §3 issuer row, the §4 `frozen` mapping and feature list, the §5 `freeze` / `unfreeze` rows) is superseded and kept only for audit comparison. Implemented in 714366d (tag `ai-baseline-d5`) and reviewed before merge; see [D5 implementation and review](../d5-implementation.md). *Superseded sentence: "Until the code lands, the D5 functions describe intended behaviour, not implemented behaviour."* A consequence for the §1 trust model: anyone the issuer grants `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` can now force-transfer revoked holdings, so that grant extends the issuer's trust to them.
10	
11	Phase 4 update (28 October 2026): the later [Phase 4 requirements](phase4-requirements.md) authorise building the frontend against the already implemented contracts and prohibit unnecessary Solidity redesign. They supersede the historical instruction to block Phase 4 on D5. Pause/freeze/forced transfer remain unsupported and are not fabricated in the UI. See [Phase 4 implementation and verification limits](../phase4-implementation.md). *(Note added at the D5 merge, 4 November 2026: this was true when written. Pause and forced transfer are now implemented on the contract. The UI still has no controls for them, but its history shows forced transfers (AUD-013).)*
12	
13	How this version was produced: human decisions, with AI-assisted research. The research sessions are logged in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Changes from `spec-v0.md` are explained in section 10.
14	
15	## 1. Problem and trust model
16	
17	**Problem**: real-world asset ownership is opaque, settlement is slow, and compliance tracking is manual. Traditional fund administration relies on intermediaries for record-keeping, transfer approval, and settlement, introducing delay and counterparty risk.
18	
19	**Why a blockchain**: an Ethereum smart contract provides an immutable, publicly auditable share register. Transfer rules (whitelist, freeze, pause) are enforced in code rather than by a custodian. Settlement is atomic — a buyer pays ETH and receives tokens in a single transaction, eliminating counterparty risk. No intermediary can alter the ownership record.
20	
21	**Trust model**: the issuer is trusted to correctly describe the off-chain asset and to maintain the legal register that backs the tokens. The on-chain token is a share register only — the legal claim (e.g. beneficial interest in the fund) sits off-chain in a subscription agreement. The platform admin is trusted to authorise only legitimate issuers.
22	
23	**Out of trust scope**: oracle price accuracy, issuer solvency, off-chain legal enforceability.
24	
25	## 2. Asset and scope
26	
27	Instrument: **fictional real estate investment fund** — Campus Property Fund.
28	
29	| Field | Value |
30	|---|---|
31	| Token name | Campus Property Token |
32	| Symbol | CPT |
33	| Total supply | 10 000 CPT |
34	| Token decimals | 0 (whole units) |
35	| Initial sale price | 0.001 testnet ETH / token |
36	| Issuer | MetaMask Wallet A |
37	| Investor 1 | MetaMask Wallet B |
38	| Investor 2 | MetaMask Wallet C |
39	
40	A second demo asset, Digital Licensing Revenue Pool (symbol: DLP), will be deployed using the same contracts with different metadata to demonstrate the multi-asset registry.
41	
42	Both assets are ERC-20 tokens representing fractional interests in a fictional fund. Tokenising unique NFTs or enforcing actual intellectual-property rights is out of scope.
43	
44	## 3. Roles
45	
46	| Actor | Can | Cannot |
47	|---|---|---|
48	| Platform admin | authorise issuer wallets; deauthorise issuer wallets | hold tokens; buy assets |
49	| Authorised issuer | create assets (sets token name, symbol, supply, sale price at creation); whitelist investor addresses; allocate tokens to the sale contract; withdraw ETH proceeds from the sale contract; freeze an individual investor address; unfreeze; pause all transfers; unpause | control another issuer's asset; change the sale price after creation |
50	| Investor | connect wallet; buy tokens from the sale contract (if whitelisted); transfer tokens to another whitelisted address; view own balance | buy if not whitelisted; transfer to non-whitelisted address |
51	
52	An issuer cannot modify the whitelist, freeze state, or pause state of a token they did not deploy.
53	
54	## 4. Contracts and state
55	
56	### AssetToken.sol
57	
58	Purpose: ERC-20 token with compliance controls.
59	
60	State variables:
61	- `address public issuer` — set at deployment, immutable in practice
62	- `mapping(address => bool) public whitelist` — addresses permitted to hold and transfer tokens
63	- `bool public paused` — when true, all transfers revert
64	- `mapping(address => bool) public frozen` — individual addresses barred from sending or receiving
65	
66	Calls: none external (pure ERC-20 logic + compliance hooks).
67	
68	**Price model**: fixed price set at deployment, stored in AssetSale (not AssetToken). AssetToken has no knowledge of price.
69	
70	**Extra features in scope**: whitelist (required to receive or send), pause (issuer halts all transfers globally), freeze (issuer bars one address), forced transfer (issuer can move tokens out of a frozen address to recover them).
71	
72	**Out of scope for AssetToken**: redemption, yield/dividend, NAV oracle, upgradeability.
73	
74	### AssetFactory.sol
75	
76	Purpose: authorise issuers; deploy and register asset contracts.
77	
78	State variables:
79	- `address public admin` — platform admin, set in constructor
80	- `mapping(address => bool) public authorisedIssuers`
81	- `address[] public assets` — list of all deployed AssetToken addresses
82	- `mapping(address => address) public tokenToSale` — maps each AssetToken to its AssetSale
83	
84	Calls: deploys `AssetToken` and `AssetSale`.
85	
86	### AssetSale.sol
87	
88	Purpose: hold sale inventory; accept fixed-price ETH payments; hold proceeds for issuer withdrawal.
89	
90	State variables:
91	- `AssetToken public token`
92	- `uint256 public priceWei` — fixed price per token in wei, set at deployment
93	- `address public issuer`
94	
95	**DvP design**: escrow. The issuer calls `allocate(amount)`, transferring tokens from their wallet into the AssetSale contract. A buyer calls `buy(amount)` with `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; tokens transfer to the buyer immediately and ETH is held in the contract. The issuer later calls `withdrawProceeds()` to collect ETH.
96	
97	**Subscription flow**: instant. `buy` reverts if the caller is not whitelisted or if the contract holds fewer tokens than requested; otherwise the transfer is immediate with no approval queue.
98	
99	**Reentrancy requirement**: `withdrawProceeds` must use the checks-effects-interactions pattern — zero the internal ETH balance before calling out — or apply a reentrancy guard. An issuer whose address is a contract could otherwise re-enter and drain more ETH than owed.
100	
101	## 5. Functions
102	
103	Every external function, who may call it, preconditions, effects, events emitted, and what must revert.
104	
105	| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
106	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
107	| `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | — | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = true` | `IssuerAuthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr already authorised |
108	| `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | addr is authorised | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = false` | `IssuerDeauthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr not authorised. **Note**: deauthorisation prevents future calls to `createAsset` only. Existing deployed AssetToken and AssetSale contracts continue operating; the admin cannot revoke an issuer's authority over contracts they have already deployed. |
109	| `AssetFactory.createAsset(name, symbol, supply, priceWei)` | authorised issuer | priceWei > 0; supply > 0 | deploys AssetToken, mints supply to issuer; deploys AssetSale; records both in registry | `AssetCreated(token, sale, issuer)` | caller not authorised |
110	| `AssetToken.addToWhitelist(address)` | issuer | — | `whitelist[addr] = true` | `Whitelisted(addr)` | caller != issuer |
111	| `AssetToken.removeFromWhitelist(address)` | issuer | addr has zero balance | `whitelist[addr] = false` | `RemovedFromWhitelist(addr)` | caller != issuer; addr has non-zero balance. **Recovery flow when addr is frozen**: issuer must (1) call `forcedTransfer(addr, safeAddr, balance)` to empty addr's holdings, then (2) call `removeFromWhitelist(addr)`. |
112	| `AssetToken.transfer(to, amount)` | token holder | `whitelist[to]`; `!paused`; `!frozen[from]`; `!frozen[to]` | standard ERC-20 transfer | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` | any precondition false |
113	| `AssetToken.transferFrom(from, to, amount)` | approved spender | same as transfer | same as transfer | `Transfer` | any precondition false |
114	| `AssetToken.pause()` | issuer | `!paused` | `paused = true` | `Paused()` | caller != issuer; already paused |
115	| `AssetToken.unpause()` | issuer | `paused` | `paused = false` | `Unpaused()` | caller != issuer; not paused |
116	| `AssetToken.freeze(address)` | issuer | `!frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = true` | `Frozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; already frozen |
117	| `AssetToken.unfreeze(address)` | issuer | `frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = false` | `Unfrozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; not frozen |
118	| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | issuer | `whitelist[to]`; `!frozen[to]` | transfers regardless of `frozen[from]` and regardless of `paused` — this is the issuer's emergency recovery mechanism | `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller != issuer; `to` not whitelisted; `to` is frozen |
119	| `AssetSale.allocate(uint256 amount)` | issuer | issuer ERC-20 balance >= amount; issuer has approved AssetSale | transfers tokens from issuer to AssetSale | `Allocated(amount)` | caller != issuer; balance insufficient |
120	| `AssetSale.buy(uint256 amount)` | investor | `whitelist[msg.sender]`; `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; AssetSale token balance >= amount | transfers tokens to buyer; ETH held in contract | `Purchased(buyer, amount)` | any precondition false |
121	| `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | ETH balance > 0 | sends full ETH balance to issuer | `ProceedsWithdrawn(amount)` | caller != issuer; no ETH to withdraw |
122	
123	### D5 functions (decided 3 November 2026; these supersede the `pause`, `unpause`, `freeze`, `unfreeze` and `forcedTransfer` rows above)
124	
125	"Admin" here means a holder of `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` on that AssetToken. The issuer always holds this role (D6).
126	
127	| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
128	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
129	| `AssetToken.pause()` | admin | not paused | paused. Every token movement except `forcedTransfer` now reverts: `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and through them `AssetSale.allocate`, `buyTokens` and `recoverUnsoldTokens` | `Paused(account)` (OpenZeppelin `Pausable`) | caller is not admin; already paused |
130	| `AssetToken.unpause()` | admin | paused | unpaused | `Unpaused(account)` (OpenZeppelin `Pausable`) | caller is not admin; not paused |
131	| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | admin | `from` is not the zero address; `from` is not whitelisted (its eligibility was revoked); `to` is whitelisted | moves `amount` from `from` to `to`, whether or not the token is paused. `totalSupply` is unchanged | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` and `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller is not admin; `from` is the zero address; `from` is whitelisted; `to` is not whitelisted; `amount` exceeds `from`'s balance |
132	
133	Recovery flow (for a lost key, or after a compliance removal): the admin calls `setWhitelisted(from, false)`, then `forcedTransfer(from, safeAddr, balance)`. Requiring revocation first means a live investor or the sale contract cannot be drained without an earlier `WhitelistUpdated` event on chain. The zero-address check is needed because OpenZeppelin's `_update` treats a move from `address(0)` as a mint. `address(0)` is never whitelisted, so without the check `forcedTransfer` could create tokens.
134	
135	## 6. Invariants
136	
137	Properties that must hold after any sequence of calls. These become invariant and unit tests.
138	
139	1. **Eligibility invariant** (restated by AUD-005, then by D5): every token movement (`transfer`, `transferFrom`, a sale purchase) has a whitelisted sender and a whitelisted recipient. The one exception is `forcedTransfer`, whose sender must *not* be whitelisted (invariant 6). A holder whose eligibility is revoked keeps their balance unless the admin force-transfers it. Until re-approved, they can neither send, receive nor buy. *Superseded wording (AUD-005), kept for audit comparison: "every token movement — `transfer`, `transferFrom`, a sale purchase — has a whitelisted sender and a whitelisted recipient. A holder whose eligibility is revoked keeps their balance but can neither send nor receive, nor buy, until re-approved." Original wording: "every address with a non-zero CPT balance is on the whitelist (`balanceOf(addr) > 0 → whitelist[addr] == true`)". That cannot hold since Phase 2 §2.3, which requires revocation to preserve balances.*
140	2. **Supply invariant**: `totalSupply()` equals the sum of all individual balances at all times.
141	3. **Sale proceeds invariant** (restated by AUD-007, decision D7): `unclaimedProceeds` equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus the total withdrawn by the issuer, and is ≤ the ETH balance of AssetSale. Any excess is ETH forced in by `selfdestruct` or a coinbase reward, and the issuer can recover it with `sweepExcessETH()`. *Superseded wording: "ETH held by AssetSale equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus total ETH withdrawn by the issuer". That cannot be guaranteed, because ETH can be forced into any contract.*
142	4. **Transfer gate invariant**: no transfer to a non-whitelisted address ever succeeds; every such attempt reverts.
143	5. **Pause invariant** (restated by D5): while the token is paused, no token movement succeeds except `forcedTransfer` called by an admin. That includes `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and AssetSale's `allocate`, `buyTokens` and `recoverUnsoldTokens`. *Superseded wording: "when `paused == true`, no `transfer` or `transferFrom` succeeds (except `forcedTransfer` by issuer)".*
144	6. **Forced-transfer invariant** (replaces the freeze invariant, D5): `forcedTransfer` only succeeds when the caller holds `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, `from` is a non-zero address that is not whitelisted, and `to` is whitelisted. It never changes `totalSupply`. *Superseded freeze invariant: "when `frozen[addr] == true`, `addr` cannot send tokens via `transfer` or `transferFrom`". Under D5 that property is covered by invariant 1, because a revoked address cannot send.*
145	7. **Issuer isolation invariant**: address X can only call `addToWhitelist`, `pause`, `forcedTransfer`, `allocate`, or `withdrawProceeds` on an AssetToken / AssetSale that X deployed. (`freeze` was removed from this list by D5.)
146	8. **Reentrancy invariant**: after `withdrawProceeds` completes, the ETH balance tracked by AssetSale is zero, regardless of any re-entrant calls made during the ETH send. Implementation must zero the balance before the external call.
147	
148	## 7. Frontend
149	
150	**Admin dashboard** (`/admin`)
151	- Shows: list of authorised issuers (from `AssetFactory`)
152	- Actions: authorise new issuer (enter address → `authoriseIssuer`); deauthorise (→ `deauthoriseIssuer`)
153	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.authorisedIssuers`, `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer`, `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer`
154	
155	**Issuer dashboard** (`/issuer`)
156	- Shows: list of assets the connected wallet deployed; per-asset: token balance, AssetSale inventory, ETH proceeds
157	- Actions: create new asset (form: name, symbol, supply, price → `createAsset`); allocate tokens (enter amount → approve then `allocate`); whitelist investor (enter address → `addToWhitelist`); withdraw proceeds (→ `withdrawProceeds`)
158	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.createAsset`, `AssetToken.addToWhitelist`, `AssetSale.allocate`, `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds`
159	
160	**Investor dashboard** (`/investor`)
161	- Shows: all assets in factory registry; for each: name, symbol, price, available tokens; own holdings
162	- Actions: buy tokens (enter amount, pay ETH → `buy`); transfer tokens (enter recipient + amount → `transfer`)
163	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.assets`, `AssetSale.buy`, `AssetToken.transfer`
164	
165	Each page connects via MetaMask using ethers.js `BrowserProvider`. Deployed contract addresses are read from a JSON config file generated by the deploy script.
166	
167	## 8. Out of scope
168	
169	- NFT-based unique assets — per-asset complexity out of MVP scope
170	- Redemption / buyback — out of scope
171	- Yield / dividend distribution — out of scope
172	- NAV oracle or price updates after creation — out of scope; price is fixed at deployment
173	- Multi-jurisdiction compliance rules beyond a single whitelist — out of scope
174	- Actual legal enforceability of the on-chain record — out of scope
175	- Governance or on-chain voting — out of scope
176	- Gas optimisation for large investor sets — out of scope for MVP
177	
178	## 9. Assumptions
179	
180	- Network: Sepolia testnet (chain ID 11155111) for integration; Hardhat local network (chain ID 31337) for development

# Spec v1: frozen specification

Status: FROZEN. No `TODO(decision)` markers remain.

Phase 2 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 2 requirements](phase2-requirements.md) govern token implementation where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, AccessControl delegates compliance administration, revoking eligibility preserves existing balances, and pause/freeze/forced transfer are not implemented in this phase. See [implementation decisions](../phase2-implementation.md) for the exact API and scope. The original requirements below remain preserved for audit comparison.

Phase 3 update (23 October 2026): the user's later [Phase 3 requirements](phase3-requirements.md) govern AssetFactory and AssetSale where they differ from this historical specification. In particular, the function names change (`authorizeIssuer`, `revokeIssuer`, `buyTokens`, `pricePerToken`), the registry gains `getAsset` / `getAssetCount` with description and asset-type metadata, and a sale can be closed so unsold inventory can be recovered. The decisions are recorded in that file. The reentrancy requirement and invariant 8 below still apply.

Decision D5 (opened 23 October 2026 in [phase3-requirements.md](phase3-requirements.md); decided 3 November 2026): **pause and forced transfer are implemented; freeze is dropped.** Freeze adds nothing because whitelist revocation already does the same job. Since Phase 2 §2.3, a revoked holder keeps their balance but can neither send, receive nor buy (invariant 1). So "freeze" in this spec now means revoking eligibility with `setWhitelisted(addr, false)`. The governing function rows are in §5 under "D5 functions", and invariants 1, 5, 6 and 7 are restated. Everywhere else, a mention of freeze (§1 "Why a blockchain", the §3 issuer row, the §4 `frozen` mapping and feature list, the §5 `freeze` / `unfreeze` rows) is superseded and kept only for audit comparison. Implemented in 714366d (tag `ai-baseline-d5`) and reviewed before merge; see [D5 implementation and review](../d5-implementation.md). *Superseded sentence: "Until the code lands, the D5 functions describe intended behaviour, not implemented behaviour."* A consequence for the §1 trust model: anyone the issuer grants `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` can now force-transfer revoked holdings, so that grant extends the issuer's trust to them.

Phase 4 update (28 October 2026): the later [Phase 4 requirements](phase4-requirements.md) authorise building the frontend against the already implemented contracts and prohibit unnecessary Solidity redesign. They supersede the historical instruction to block Phase 4 on D5. Pause/freeze/forced transfer remain unsupported and are not fabricated in the UI. See [Phase 4 implementation and verification limits](../phase4-implementation.md). *(Note added at the D5 merge, 4 November 2026: this was true when written. Pause and forced transfer are now implemented on the contract. The UI still has no controls for them, but its history shows forced transfers (AUD-013).)*

How this version was produced: human decisions, with AI-assisted research. The research sessions are logged in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Changes from `spec-v0.md` are explained in section 10.

## 1. Problem and trust model

**Problem**: real-world asset ownership is opaque, settlement is slow, and compliance tracking is manual. Traditional fund administration relies on intermediaries for record-keeping, transfer approval, and settlement, introducing delay and counterparty risk.

**Why a blockchain**: an Ethereum smart contract provides an immutable, publicly auditable share register. Transfer rules (whitelist, freeze, pause) are enforced in code rather than by a custodian. Settlement is atomic — a buyer pays ETH and receives tokens in a single transaction, eliminating counterparty risk. No intermediary can alter the ownership record.

**Trust model**: the issuer is trusted to correctly describe the off-chain asset and to maintain the legal register that backs the tokens. The on-chain token is a share register only — the legal claim (e.g. beneficial interest in the fund) sits off-chain in a subscription agreement. The platform admin is trusted to authorise only legitimate issuers.

**Out of trust scope**: oracle price accuracy, issuer solvency, off-chain legal enforceability.

## 2. Asset and scope

Instrument: **fictional real estate investment fund** — Campus Property Fund.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Token name | Campus Property Token |
| Symbol | CPT |
| Total supply | 10 000 CPT |
| Token decimals | 0 (whole units) |
| Initial sale price | 0.001 testnet ETH / token |
| Issuer | MetaMask Wallet A |
| Investor 1 | MetaMask Wallet B |
| Investor 2 | MetaMask Wallet C |

A second demo asset, Digital Licensing Revenue Pool (symbol: DLP), will be deployed using the same contracts with different metadata to demonstrate the multi-asset registry.

Both assets are ERC-20 tokens representing fractional interests in a fictional fund. Tokenising unique NFTs or enforcing actual intellectual-property rights is out of scope.

## 3. Roles

| Actor | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Platform admin | authorise issuer wallets; deauthorise issuer wallets | hold tokens; buy assets |
| Authorised issuer | create assets (sets token name, symbol, supply, sale price at creation); whitelist investor addresses; allocate tokens to the sale contract; withdraw ETH proceeds from the sale contract; freeze an individual investor address; unfreeze; pause all transfers; unpause | control another issuer's asset; change the sale price after creation |
| Investor | connect wallet; buy tokens from the sale contract (if whitelisted); transfer tokens to another whitelisted address; view own balance | buy if not whitelisted; transfer to non-whitelisted address |

An issuer cannot modify the whitelist, freeze state, or pause state of a token they did not deploy.

## 4. Contracts and state

### AssetToken.sol

Purpose: ERC-20 token with compliance controls.

State variables:
- `address public issuer` — set at deployment, immutable in practice
- `mapping(address => bool) public whitelist` — addresses permitted to hold and transfer tokens
- `bool public paused` — when true, all transfers revert
- `mapping(address => bool) public frozen` — individual addresses barred from sending or receiving

Calls: none external (pure ERC-20 logic + compliance hooks).

**Price model**: fixed price set at deployment, stored in AssetSale (not AssetToken). AssetToken has no knowledge of price.

**Extra features in scope**: whitelist (required to receive or send), pause (issuer halts all transfers globally), freeze (issuer bars one address), forced transfer (issuer can move tokens out of a frozen address to recover them).

**Out of scope for AssetToken**: redemption, yield/dividend, NAV oracle, upgradeability.

### AssetFactory.sol

Purpose: authorise issuers; deploy and register asset contracts.

State variables:
- `address public admin` — platform admin, set in constructor
- `mapping(address => bool) public authorisedIssuers`
- `address[] public assets` — list of all deployed AssetToken addresses
- `mapping(address => address) public tokenToSale` — maps each AssetToken to its AssetSale

Calls: deploys `AssetToken` and `AssetSale`.

### AssetSale.sol

Purpose: hold sale inventory; accept fixed-price ETH payments; hold proceeds for issuer withdrawal.

State variables:
- `AssetToken public token`
- `uint256 public priceWei` — fixed price per token in wei, set at deployment
- `address public issuer`

**DvP design**: escrow. The issuer calls `allocate(amount)`, transferring tokens from their wallet into the AssetSale contract. A buyer calls `buy(amount)` with `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; tokens transfer to the buyer immediately and ETH is held in the contract. The issuer later calls `withdrawProceeds()` to collect ETH.

**Subscription flow**: instant. `buy` reverts if the caller is not whitelisted or if the contract holds fewer tokens than requested; otherwise the transfer is immediate with no approval queue.

**Reentrancy requirement**: `withdrawProceeds` must use the checks-effects-interactions pattern — zero the internal ETH balance before calling out — or apply a reentrancy guard. An issuer whose address is a contract could otherwise re-enter and drain more ETH than owed.

## 5. Functions

Every external function, who may call it, preconditions, effects, events emitted, and what must revert.

| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | — | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = true` | `IssuerAuthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr already authorised |
| `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | addr is authorised | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = false` | `IssuerDeauthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr not authorised. **Note**: deauthorisation prevents future calls to `createAsset` only. Existing deployed AssetToken and AssetSale contracts continue operating; the admin cannot revoke an issuer's authority over contracts they have already deployed. |
| `AssetFactory.createAsset(name, symbol, supply, priceWei)` | authorised issuer | priceWei > 0; supply > 0 | deploys AssetToken, mints supply to issuer; deploys AssetSale; records both in registry | `AssetCreated(token, sale, issuer)` | caller not authorised |
| `AssetToken.addToWhitelist(address)` | issuer | — | `whitelist[addr] = true` | `Whitelisted(addr)` | caller != issuer |
| `AssetToken.removeFromWhitelist(address)` | issuer | addr has zero balance | `whitelist[addr] = false` | `RemovedFromWhitelist(addr)` | caller != issuer; addr has non-zero balance. **Recovery flow when addr is frozen**: issuer must (1) call `forcedTransfer(addr, safeAddr, balance)` to empty addr's holdings, then (2) call `removeFromWhitelist(addr)`. |
| `AssetToken.transfer(to, amount)` | token holder | `whitelist[to]`; `!paused`; `!frozen[from]`; `!frozen[to]` | standard ERC-20 transfer | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` | any precondition false |
| `AssetToken.transferFrom(from, to, amount)` | approved spender | same as transfer | same as transfer | `Transfer` | any precondition false |
| `AssetToken.pause()` | issuer | `!paused` | `paused = true` | `Paused()` | caller != issuer; already paused |
| `AssetToken.unpause()` | issuer | `paused` | `paused = false` | `Unpaused()` | caller != issuer; not paused |
| `AssetToken.freeze(address)` | issuer | `!frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = true` | `Frozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; already frozen |
| `AssetToken.unfreeze(address)` | issuer | `frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = false` | `Unfrozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; not frozen |
| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | issuer | `whitelist[to]`; `!frozen[to]` | transfers regardless of `frozen[from]` and regardless of `paused` — this is the issuer's emergency recovery mechanism | `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller != issuer; `to` not whitelisted; `to` is frozen |
| `AssetSale.allocate(uint256 amount)` | issuer | issuer ERC-20 balance >= amount; issuer has approved AssetSale | transfers tokens from issuer to AssetSale | `Allocated(amount)` | caller != issuer; balance insufficient |
| `AssetSale.buy(uint256 amount)` | investor | `whitelist[msg.sender]`; `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; AssetSale token balance >= amount | transfers tokens to buyer; ETH held in contract | `Purchased(buyer, amount)` | any precondition false |
| `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | ETH balance > 0 | sends full ETH balance to issuer | `ProceedsWithdrawn(amount)` | caller != issuer; no ETH to withdraw |

### D5 functions (decided 3 November 2026; these supersede the `pause`, `unpause`, `freeze`, `unfreeze` and `forcedTransfer` rows above)

"Admin" here means a holder of `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` on that AssetToken. The issuer always holds this role (D6).

| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AssetToken.pause()` | admin | not paused | paused. Every token movement except `forcedTransfer` now reverts: `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and through them `AssetSale.allocate`, `buyTokens` and `recoverUnsoldTokens` | `Paused(account)` (OpenZeppelin `Pausable`) | caller is not admin; already paused |
| `AssetToken.unpause()` | admin | paused | unpaused | `Unpaused(account)` (OpenZeppelin `Pausable`) | caller is not admin; not paused |
| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | admin | `from` is not the zero address; `from` is not whitelisted (its eligibility was revoked); `to` is whitelisted | moves `amount` from `from` to `to`, whether or not the token is paused. `totalSupply` is unchanged | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` and `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller is not admin; `from` is the zero address; `from` is whitelisted; `to` is not whitelisted; `amount` exceeds `from`'s balance |

Recovery flow (for a lost key, or after a compliance removal): the admin calls `setWhitelisted(from, false)`, then `forcedTransfer(from, safeAddr, balance)`. Requiring revocation first means a live investor or the sale contract cannot be drained without an earlier `WhitelistUpdated` event on chain. The zero-address check is needed because OpenZeppelin's `_update` treats a move from `address(0)` as a mint. `address(0)` is never whitelisted, so without the check `forcedTransfer` could create tokens.

## 6. Invariants

Properties that must hold after any sequence of calls. These become invariant and unit tests.

1. **Eligibility invariant** (restated by AUD-005, then by D5): every token movement (`transfer`, `transferFrom`, a sale purchase) has a whitelisted sender and a whitelisted recipient. The one exception is `forcedTransfer`, whose sender must *not* be whitelisted (invariant 6). A holder whose eligibility is revoked keeps their balance unless the admin force-transfers it. Until re-approved, they can neither send, receive nor buy. *Superseded wording (AUD-005), kept for audit comparison: "every token movement — `transfer`, `transferFrom`, a sale purchase — has a whitelisted sender and a whitelisted recipient. A holder whose eligibility is revoked keeps their balance but can neither send nor receive, nor buy, until re-approved." Original wording: "every address with a non-zero CPT balance is on the whitelist (`balanceOf(addr) > 0 → whitelist[addr] == true`)". That cannot hold since Phase 2 §2.3, which requires revocation to preserve balances.*
2. **Supply invariant**: `totalSupply()` equals the sum of all individual balances at all times.
3. **Sale proceeds invariant** (restated by AUD-007, decision D7): `unclaimedProceeds` equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus the total withdrawn by the issuer, and is ≤ the ETH balance of AssetSale. Any excess is ETH forced in by `selfdestruct` or a coinbase reward, and the issuer can recover it with `sweepExcessETH()`. *Superseded wording: "ETH held by AssetSale equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus total ETH withdrawn by the issuer". That cannot be guaranteed, because ETH can be forced into any contract.*
4. **Transfer gate invariant**: no transfer to a non-whitelisted address ever succeeds; every such attempt reverts.
5. **Pause invariant** (restated by D5): while the token is paused, no token movement succeeds except `forcedTransfer` called by an admin. That includes `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and AssetSale's `allocate`, `buyTokens` and `recoverUnsoldTokens`. *Superseded wording: "when `paused == true`, no `transfer` or `transferFrom` succeeds (except `forcedTransfer` by issuer)".*
6. **Forced-transfer invariant** (replaces the freeze invariant, D5): `forcedTransfer` only succeeds when the caller holds `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, `from` is a non-zero address that is not whitelisted, and `to` is whitelisted. It never changes `totalSupply`. *Superseded freeze invariant: "when `frozen[addr] == true`, `addr` cannot send tokens via `transfer` or `transferFrom`". Under D5 that property is covered by invariant 1, because a revoked address cannot send.*
7. **Issuer isolation invariant**: address X can only call `addToWhitelist`, `pause`, `forcedTransfer`, `allocate`, or `withdrawProceeds` on an AssetToken / AssetSale that X deployed. (`freeze` was removed from this list by D5.)
8. **Reentrancy invariant**: after `withdrawProceeds` completes, the ETH balance tracked by AssetSale is zero, regardless of any re-entrant calls made during the ETH send. Implementation must zero the balance before the external call.

## 7. Frontend

**Admin dashboard** (`/admin`)
- Shows: list of authorised issuers (from `AssetFactory`)
- Actions: authorise new issuer (enter address → `authoriseIssuer`); deauthorise (→ `deauthoriseIssuer`)
- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.authorisedIssuers`, `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer`, `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer`

**Issuer dashboard** (`/issuer`)
- Shows: list of assets the connected wallet deployed; per-asset: token balance, AssetSale inventory, ETH proceeds
- Actions: create new asset (form: name, symbol, supply, price → `createAsset`); allocate tokens (enter amount → approve then `allocate`); whitelist investor (enter address → `addToWhitelist`); withdraw proceeds (→ `withdrawProceeds`)
- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.createAsset`, `AssetToken.addToWhitelist`, `AssetSale.allocate`, `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds`

**Investor dashboard** (`/investor`)
- Shows: all assets in factory registry; for each: name, symbol, price, available tokens; own holdings
- Actions: buy tokens (enter amount, pay ETH → `buy`); transfer tokens (enter recipient + amount → `transfer`)
- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.assets`, `AssetSale.buy`, `AssetToken.transfer`

Each page connects via MetaMask using ethers.js `BrowserProvider`. Deployed contract addresses are read from a JSON config file generated by the deploy script.

## 8. Out of scope

- NFT-based unique assets — per-asset complexity out of MVP scope
- Redemption / buyback — out of scope
- Yield / dividend distribution — out of scope
- NAV oracle or price updates after creation — out of scope; price is fixed at deployment
- Multi-jurisdiction compliance rules beyond a single whitelist — out of scope
- Actual legal enforceability of the on-chain record — out of scope
- Governance or on-chain voting — out of scope
- Gas optimisation for large investor sets — out of scope for MVP

## 9. Assumptions

- Network: Sepolia testnet (chain ID 11155111) for integration; Hardhat local network (chain ID 31337) for development
- Token decimals: 0 — whole units only, consistent with fractional-unit model where each token represents one equal share
- Test wallets: three Hardhat accounts (index 0 = admin, 1 = issuer, 2 = investor) for local tests; three MetaMask burner wallets on Sepolia for demo
- Toolchain: Node.js ≥ 18, Hardhat 3.x (installed: 3.21.0), OpenZeppelin Contracts 5.x (installed: 5.6.1), ethers.js 6.x
- Frontend: React 18, Vite, ethers.js 6.x
- `.env` holds `TESTNET_RPC_URL`, `PRIVATE_KEY`, `ETHERSCAN_API_KEY` — never committed

## 10. Changes from v0

AI influence is classified from the research transcript (`docs/ai-logs/exports/2026-10-23-claude-ai-research.md`, cited as R<line>):
- **AI proposed, human adopted**: the AI recommended this and we took it.
- **AI offered, human chose otherwise**: the AI laid out options and we picked a different one.
- **No AI proposal found**: the transcript does not contain it.

Audit-1 finding F-07 showed the earlier "No" values were wrong. That "correction" (commit a609765) had itself been proposed by the Phase 1 AI session, `phase1-setup.txt` lines 1860–1867. The superseded values remain in git history.

| Change | Why | AI influence |
|---|---|---|
| Narrowed scope to one real-estate fund + one digital asset | Keeps MVP deliverable within project timeline | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI recommended a tokenised money-market fund, with a bond and gold as alternatives (R240–244). |
| Defined three concrete contracts (AssetToken, AssetFactory, AssetSale) | Makes responsibilities and security boundaries explicit | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI proposed an ERC-3643-style split: IdentityRegistry, ComplianceRules, AssetToken, Issuance, DvPSettlement (R62–66, R304–310). We chose three contracts. The name `AssetToken` matches the AI's proposal (R64). |
| Fixed sale price set at deployment (not issuer-set NAV) | Eliminates price oracle dependency; simplifies MVP | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI recommended issuer-set NAV and listed a fixed price as the simpler option (R265–267). |
| Instant subscription flow (not request-and-approve) | Reduces contract complexity; investor experience is clearer | AI proposed, human adopted (R270). |
| Escrow DvP in AssetSale (spec-v1 §4) | Sale contract holds inventory and proceeds | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI recommended approve-based DvP without escrow (R258–259). |
| Whitelist + pause + freeze + forced transfer as in-scope features | Directly addresses the "permissioning and compliance" requirement from v0 | AI proposed, human adopted. Freeze, forced transfer and pause were all rated "Must" (R296–297). D5 (3 November 2026) kept pause and forced transfer and dropped freeze, because whitelist revocation already does what freeze would. That narrowing was AI proposed, human adopted, in a Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) session. |
| Frontend split into three role-based dashboards | Matches the three-role model; each role sees only relevant actions | No AI proposal found. The AI suggested a different role split: Issuer, Compliance Agent, Investor (R310). |

3	The text below is the user's Phase 3 request, given to Claude Code on 23 October 2026. Table formatting was lost when it was pasted and has been restored as Markdown; the wording is unchanged. The decisions in the final section were made by the user in the same session, in answer to questions raised by Claude Code about conflicts with `spec-v1.md`.
4	
5	---
6	
7	Deliverable: Functional on-chain asset issuance and purchase
8	
9	Objective: Let authorised issuers create multiple tokenised assets and sell them to eligible investors.
10	
11	This is where your project develops beyond a simple ERC-20 token demonstration.
12	
13	## Task 3.1 — Implement AssetFactory.sol
14	
15	The factory will act as the entry point for new asset issuance.
16	
17	It should provide these functions:
18	
19	| Function | Purpose |
20	|---|---|
21	| `authorizeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin grants issuer permission |
22	| `revokeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin removes issuer creation permission |
23	| `createAsset(...)` | Authorised issuer creates an asset |
24	| `getAsset(assetId)` | Returns asset metadata and contract addresses |
25	| `getAssetCount()` | Returns number of registered assets |
26	
27	A successful `createAsset()` should deploy an AssetToken and associated AssetSale, then record the asset in the registry.
28	
29	Suggested metadata:
30	
31	```text
32	assetId
33	name
34	symbol
35	description
36	assetType
37	totalSupply
38	tokenContract
39	saleContract
40	issuerAddress
41	unitPriceWei
42	```
43	
44	The asset ID should be generated automatically rather than supplied by the issuer.
45	
46	## Task 3.2 — Implement AssetSale.sol
47	
48	This contract will facilitate primary-market purchases.
49	
50	Essential variables:
51	
52	```solidity
53	IERC20 public assetToken;
54	address public issuer;
55	uint256 public pricePerToken;
56	```
57	
58	Main function:
59	
60	```solidity
61	buyTokens(uint256 quantity) external payable
62	```
63	
64	Purchase validation must confirm:
65	
66	- The buyer is an approved investor.
67	- Quantity is greater than zero.
68	- Enough tokens remain in the sale contract.
69	- `msg.value` equals `quantity * pricePerToken`.
70	
71	If every condition passes, the contract transfers tokens to the investor and records the purchase event.
72	
73	Use exact payment for the MVP; partial payments, complex refunds and variable pricing are unnecessary.
74	
75	## Task 3.3 — Implement the inventory funding process
76	
77	The issuer must allocate tokens to the sale contract before buyers can purchase them.
78	
79	The lifecycle will be:
80	
81	| Step | Result |
82	|---|---|
83	| Issuer creates an asset | 10,000 CPT minted to issuer |
84	| Issuer whitelists the sale contract | Contract is permitted to hold and transfer CPT |
85	| Issuer deposits 5,000 CPT for sale | Sale contract now has purchasable inventory |
86	| Investor buys 100 CPT | Investor pays 0.1 testnet ETH and receives 100 CPT |
87	
88	To simplify the MVP, the price is fixed at asset creation. Later changes to the sale price are not supported.
89	
90	## Task 3.4 — Implement issuer withdrawals
91	
92	Create an issuer-only withdrawal function for sale proceeds.
93	
94	The function must prevent unauthorised withdrawals and account for reentrancy risks when sending ETH. Include a protected way to recover any unsold token inventory if the sale is closed.
95	
96	## Task 3.5 — Test factory and sale contracts
97	
98	Test the following scenarios:
99	
100	| Test case | Expected result |
101	|---|---|
102	| Unauthorised wallet creates an asset | Revert |
103	| Authorised issuer creates asset | Token and sale contracts deployed |
104	| Issuer creates two different assets | Both registered independently |
105	| Whitelisted investor buys 100 tokens | Correct ETH payment and token transfer |
106	| Investor underpays | Revert |
107	| Investor overpays | Revert |
108	| Investor buys more than inventory | Revert |
109	| Unapproved investor attempts purchase | Revert |
110	| Non-issuer withdraws proceeds | Revert |
111	
112	Phase 3 completion criteria: From a Hardhat script or console, you should be able to register an issuer, create an asset, whitelist an investor, fund the sale contract, execute a purchase and inspect the updated balances.
113	
114	You now have a working blockchain backend.

116	---
117	
118	## Additional constraints from the session brief

The factory will act as the entry point for new asset issuance.

It should provide these functions:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `authorizeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin grants issuer permission |
| `revokeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin removes issuer creation permission |
| `createAsset(...)` | Authorised issuer creates an asset |

A successful `createAsset()` should deploy an AssetToken and associated AssetSale, then record the asset in the registry.

Suggested metadata:

```text
assetId
name
symbol
description
assetType
totalSupply
tokenContract
saleContract
issuerAddress
unitPriceWei
```

The asset ID should be generated automatically rather than supplied by the issuer.

## Task 3.2 — Implement AssetSale.sol

This contract will facilitate primary-market purchases.

Essential variables:

```solidity
IERC20 public assetToken;
address public issuer;
uint256 public pricePerToken;
```

Main function:

```solidity
buyTokens(uint256 quantity) external payable
```

Purchase validation must confirm:

- The buyer is an approved investor.
- Quantity is greater than zero.
- Enough tokens remain in the sale contract.
- `msg.value` equals `quantity * pricePerToken`.

If every condition passes, the contract transfers tokens to the investor and records the purchase event.

Use exact payment for the MVP; partial payments, complex refunds and variable pricing are unnecessary.

## Task 3.3 — Implement the inventory funding process

The issuer must allocate tokens to the sale contract before buyers can purchase them.

The lifecycle will be:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Issuer creates an asset | 10,000 CPT minted to issuer |
| Issuer whitelists the sale contract | Contract is permitted to hold and transfer CPT |
| Issuer deposits 5,000 CPT for sale | Sale contract now has purchasable inventory |
| Investor buys 100 CPT | Investor pays 0.1 testnet ETH and receives 100 CPT |

To simplify the MVP, the price is fixed at asset creation. Later changes to the sale price are not supported.

## Task 3.4 — Implement issuer withdrawals

Create an issuer-only withdrawal function for sale proceeds.

The function must prevent unauthorised withdrawals and account for reentrancy risks when sending ETH. Include a protected way to recover any unsold token inventory if the sale is closed.

Test the following scenarios:

| Test case | Expected result |
|---|---|
| Unauthorised wallet creates an asset | Revert |
| Authorised issuer creates asset | Token and sale contracts deployed |
| Issuer creates two different assets | Both registered independently |
| Whitelisted investor buys 100 tokens | Correct ETH payment and token transfer |
| Investor underpays | Revert |
| Investor overpays | Revert |
| Investor buys more than inventory | Revert |
| Unapproved investor attempts purchase | Revert |
| Non-issuer withdraws proceeds | Revert |

You now have a working blockchain backend.

18

56	### AssetToken.sol
57	
58	Purpose: ERC-20 token with compliance controls.
59	
60	State variables:
61	- `address public issuer` — set at deployment, immutable in practice
62	- `mapping(address => bool) public whitelist` — addresses permitted to hold and transfer tokens
63	- `bool public paused` — when true, all transfers revert
64	- `mapping(address => bool) public frozen` — individual addresses barred from sending or receiving
65	
66	Calls: none external (pure ERC-20 logic + compliance hooks).
67	
68	**Price model**: fixed price set at deployment, stored in AssetSale (not AssetToken). AssetToken has no knowledge of price.
69	
70	**Extra features in scope**: whitelist (required to receive or send), pause (issuer halts all transfers globally), freeze (issuer bars one address), forced transfer (issuer can move tokens out of a frozen address to recover them).
71	
72	**Out of scope for AssetToken**: redemption, yield/dividend, NAV oracle, upgradeability.
73	
74	### AssetFactory.sol
75	
76	Purpose: authorise issuers; deploy and register asset contracts.
77	
78	State variables:
79	- `address public admin` — platform admin, set in constructor
80	- `mapping(address => bool) public authorisedIssuers`
81	- `address[] public assets` — list of all deployed AssetToken addresses
82	- `mapping(address => address) public tokenToSale` — maps each AssetToken to its AssetSale
83	
84	Calls: deploys `AssetToken` and `AssetSale`.
85	
86	### AssetSale.sol
87	
88	Purpose: hold sale inventory; accept fixed-price ETH payments; hold proceeds for issuer withdrawal.
89	
90	State variables:
91	- `AssetToken public token`
92	- `uint256 public priceWei` — fixed price per token in wei, set at deployment
93	- `address public issuer`
94	
95	**DvP design**: escrow. The issuer calls `allocate(amount)`, transferring tokens from their wallet into the AssetSale contract. A buyer calls `buy(amount)` with `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; tokens transfer to the buyer immediately and ETH is held in the contract. The issuer later calls `withdrawProceeds()` to collect ETH.
96	
97	**Subscription flow**: instant. `buy` reverts if the caller is not whitelisted or if the contract holds fewer tokens than requested; otherwise the transfer is immediate with no approval queue.
98	
99	**Reentrancy requirement**: `withdrawProceeds` must use the checks-effects-interactions pattern — zero the internal ETH balance before calling out — or apply a reentrancy guard. An issuer whose address is a contract could otherwise re-enter and drain more ETH than owed.
100	
101	## 5. Functions
102	
103	Every external function, who may call it, preconditions, effects, events emitted, and what must revert.
104	
105	| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
106	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
107	| `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | — | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = true` | `IssuerAuthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr already authorised |
108	| `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer(address)` | admin | addr is authorised | `authorisedIssuers[addr] = false` | `IssuerDeauthorised(addr)` | caller != admin; addr not authorised. **Note**: deauthorisation prevents future calls to `createAsset` only. Existing deployed AssetToken and AssetSale contracts continue operating; the admin cannot revoke an issuer's authority over contracts they have already deployed. |
109	| `AssetFactory.createAsset(name, symbol, supply, priceWei)` | authorised issuer | priceWei > 0; supply > 0 | deploys AssetToken, mints supply to issuer; deploys AssetSale; records both in registry | `AssetCreated(token, sale, issuer)` | caller not authorised |
110	| `AssetToken.addToWhitelist(address)` | issuer | — | `whitelist[addr] = true` | `Whitelisted(addr)` | caller != issuer |
111	| `AssetToken.removeFromWhitelist(address)` | issuer | addr has zero balance | `whitelist[addr] = false` | `RemovedFromWhitelist(addr)` | caller != issuer; addr has non-zero balance. **Recovery flow when addr is frozen**: issuer must (1) call `forcedTransfer(addr, safeAddr, balance)` to empty addr's holdings, then (2) call `removeFromWhitelist(addr)`. |
112	| `AssetToken.transfer(to, amount)` | token holder | `whitelist[to]`; `!paused`; `!frozen[from]`; `!frozen[to]` | standard ERC-20 transfer | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` | any precondition false |
113	| `AssetToken.transferFrom(from, to, amount)` | approved spender | same as transfer | same as transfer | `Transfer` | any precondition false |
114	| `AssetToken.pause()` | issuer | `!paused` | `paused = true` | `Paused()` | caller != issuer; already paused |
115	| `AssetToken.unpause()` | issuer | `paused` | `paused = false` | `Unpaused()` | caller != issuer; not paused |
116	| `AssetToken.freeze(address)` | issuer | `!frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = true` | `Frozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; already frozen |
117	| `AssetToken.unfreeze(address)` | issuer | `frozen[addr]` | `frozen[addr] = false` | `Unfrozen(addr)` | caller != issuer; not frozen |
118	| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | issuer | `whitelist[to]`; `!frozen[to]` | transfers regardless of `frozen[from]` and regardless of `paused` — this is the issuer's emergency recovery mechanism | `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller != issuer; `to` not whitelisted; `to` is frozen |
119	| `AssetSale.allocate(uint256 amount)` | issuer | issuer ERC-20 balance >= amount; issuer has approved AssetSale | transfers tokens from issuer to AssetSale | `Allocated(amount)` | caller != issuer; balance insufficient |
120	| `AssetSale.buy(uint256 amount)` | investor | `whitelist[msg.sender]`; `msg.value == amount * priceWei`; AssetSale token balance >= amount | transfers tokens to buyer; ETH held in contract | `Purchased(buyer, amount)` | any precondition false |
121	| `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | ETH balance > 0 | sends full ETH balance to issuer | `ProceedsWithdrawn(amount)` | caller != issuer; no ETH to withdraw |
122	
123	### D5 functions (decided 3 November 2026; these supersede the `pause`, `unpause`, `freeze`, `unfreeze` and `forcedTransfer` rows above)
124	
125	"Admin" here means a holder of `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` on that AssetToken. The issuer always holds this role (D6).
126	
127	| Function | Caller | Preconditions | Effects | Event | Reverts if |
128	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
129	| `AssetToken.pause()` | admin | not paused | paused. Every token movement except `forcedTransfer` now reverts: `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and through them `AssetSale.allocate`, `buyTokens` and `recoverUnsoldTokens` | `Paused(account)` (OpenZeppelin `Pausable`) | caller is not admin; already paused |
130	| `AssetToken.unpause()` | admin | paused | unpaused | `Unpaused(account)` (OpenZeppelin `Pausable`) | caller is not admin; not paused |
131	| `AssetToken.forcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | admin | `from` is not the zero address; `from` is not whitelisted (its eligibility was revoked); `to` is whitelisted | moves `amount` from `from` to `to`, whether or not the token is paused. `totalSupply` is unchanged | `Transfer(from, to, amount)` and `ForcedTransfer(from, to, amount)` | caller is not admin; `from` is the zero address; `from` is whitelisted; `to` is not whitelisted; `amount` exceeds `from`'s balance |
132	
133	Recovery flow (for a lost key, or after a compliance removal): the admin calls `setWhitelisted(from, false)`, then `forcedTransfer(from, safeAddr, balance)`. Requiring revocation first means a live investor or the sale contract cannot be drained without an earlier `WhitelistUpdated` event on chain. The zero-address check is needed because OpenZeppelin's `_update` treats a move from `address(0)` as a mint. `address(0)` is never whitelisted, so without the check `forcedTransfer` could create tokens.
134	
135	## 6. Invariants
136	
137	Properties that must hold after any sequence of calls. These become invariant and unit tests.
138	
139	1. **Eligibility invariant** (restated by AUD-005, then by D5): every token movement (`transfer`, `transferFrom`, a sale purchase) has a whitelisted sender and a whitelisted recipient. The one exception is `forcedTransfer`, whose sender must *not* be whitelisted (invariant 6). A holder whose eligibility is revoked keeps their balance unless the admin force-transfers it. Until re-approved, they can neither send, receive nor buy. *Superseded wording (AUD-005), kept for audit comparison: "every token movement — `transfer`, `transferFrom`, a sale purchase — has a whitelisted sender and a whitelisted recipient. A holder whose eligibility is revoked keeps their balance but can neither send nor receive, nor buy, until re-approved." Original wording: "every address with a non-zero CPT balance is on the whitelist (`balanceOf(addr) > 0 → whitelist[addr] == true`)". That cannot hold since Phase 2 §2.3, which requires revocation to preserve balances.*
140	2. **Supply invariant**: `totalSupply()` equals the sum of all individual balances at all times.
141	3. **Sale proceeds invariant** (restated by AUD-007, decision D7): `unclaimedProceeds` equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus the total withdrawn by the issuer, and is ≤ the ETH balance of AssetSale. Any excess is ETH forced in by `selfdestruct` or a coinbase reward, and the issuer can recover it with `sweepExcessETH()`. *Superseded wording: "ETH held by AssetSale equals the total ETH paid by buyers minus total ETH withdrawn by the issuer". That cannot be guaranteed, because ETH can be forced into any contract.*
142	4. **Transfer gate invariant**: no transfer to a non-whitelisted address ever succeeds; every such attempt reverts.
143	5. **Pause invariant** (restated by D5): while the token is paused, no token movement succeeds except `forcedTransfer` called by an admin. That includes `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and AssetSale's `allocate`, `buyTokens` and `recoverUnsoldTokens`. *Superseded wording: "when `paused == true`, no `transfer` or `transferFrom` succeeds (except `forcedTransfer` by issuer)".*
144	6. **Forced-transfer invariant** (replaces the freeze invariant, D5): `forcedTransfer` only succeeds when the caller holds `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, `from` is a non-zero address that is not whitelisted, and `to` is whitelisted. It never changes `totalSupply`. *Superseded freeze invariant: "when `frozen[addr] == true`, `addr` cannot send tokens via `transfer` or `transferFrom`". Under D5 that property is covered by invariant 1, because a revoked address cannot send.*
145	7. **Issuer isolation invariant**: address X can only call `addToWhitelist`, `pause`, `forcedTransfer`, `allocate`, or `withdrawProceeds` on an AssetToken / AssetSale that X deployed. (`freeze` was removed from this list by D5.)
146	8. **Reentrancy invariant**: after `withdrawProceeds` completes, the ETH balance tracked by AssetSale is zero, regardless of any re-entrant calls made during the ETH send. Implementation must zero the balance before the external call.
147	
148	## 7. Frontend
149	
150	**Admin dashboard** (`/admin`)
151	- Shows: list of authorised issuers (from `AssetFactory`)
152	- Actions: authorise new issuer (enter address → `authoriseIssuer`); deauthorise (→ `deauthoriseIssuer`)
153	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.authorisedIssuers`, `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer`, `AssetFactory.deauthoriseIssuer`
154	
155	**Issuer dashboard** (`/issuer`)
156	- Shows: list of assets the connected wallet deployed; per-asset: token balance, AssetSale inventory, ETH proceeds
157	- Actions: create new asset (form: name, symbol, supply, price → `createAsset`); allocate tokens (enter amount → approve then `allocate`); whitelist investor (enter address → `addToWhitelist`); withdraw proceeds (→ `withdrawProceeds`)
158	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.createAsset`, `AssetToken.addToWhitelist`, `AssetSale.allocate`, `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds`
159	
160	**Investor dashboard** (`/investor`)
161	- Shows: all assets in factory registry; for each: name, symbol, price, available tokens; own holdings
162	- Actions: buy tokens (enter amount, pay ETH → `buy`); transfer tokens (enter recipient + amount → `transfer`)
163	- Contract calls: `AssetFactory.assets`, `AssetSale.buy`, `AssetToken.transfer`
164	
165	Each page connects via MetaMask using ethers.js `BrowserProvider`. Deployed contract addresses are read from a JSON config file generated by the deploy script.
166	
167	## 8. Out of scope
168	
169	- NFT-based unique assets — per-asset complexity out of MVP scope
170	- Redemption / buyback — out of scope
171	- Yield / dividend distribution — out of scope
172	- NAV oracle or price updates after creation — out of scope; price is fixed at deployment
173	- Multi-jurisdiction compliance rules beyond a single whitelist — out of scope
174	- Actual legal enforceability of the on-chain record — out of scope
175	- Governance or on-chain voting — out of scope
176	- Gas optimisation for large investor sets — out of scope for MVP
177	
178	## 9. Assumptions
179	
180	- Network: Sepolia testnet (chain ID 11155111) for integration; Hardhat local network (chain ID 31337) for development
181	- Token decimals: 0 — whole units only, consistent with fractional-unit model where each token represents one equal share
182	- Test wallets: three Hardhat accounts (index 0 = admin, 1 = issuer, 2 = investor) for local tests; three MetaMask burner wallets on Sepolia for demo
183	- Toolchain: Node.js ≥ 18, Hardhat 3.x (installed: 3.21.0), OpenZeppelin Contracts 5.x (installed: 5.6.1), ethers.js 6.x
184	- Frontend: React 18, Vite, ethers.js 6.x
185	- `.env` holds `TESTNET_RPC_URL`, `PRIVATE_KEY`, `ETHERSCAN_API_KEY` — never committed
186	
187	## 10. Changes from v0
188	
189	AI influence is classified from the research transcript (`docs/ai-logs/exports/2026-10-23-claude-ai-research.md`, cited as R<line>):
190	- **AI proposed, human adopted**: the AI recommended this and we took it.
191	- **AI offered, human chose otherwise**: the AI laid out options and we picked a different one.
192	- **No AI proposal found**: the transcript does not contain it.
193	
194	Audit-1 finding F-07 showed the earlier "No" values were wrong. That "correction" (commit a609765) had itself been proposed by the Phase 1 AI session, `phase1-setup.txt` lines 1860–1867. The superseded values remain in git history.
195	
196	| Change | Why | AI influence |
197	|---|---|---|
198	| Narrowed scope to one real-estate fund + one digital asset | Keeps MVP deliverable within project timeline | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI recommended a tokenised money-market fund, with a bond and gold as alternatives (R240–244). |
199	| Defined three concrete contracts (AssetToken, AssetFactory, AssetSale) | Makes responsibilities and security boundaries explicit | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI proposed an ERC-3643-style split: IdentityRegistry, ComplianceRules, AssetToken, Issuance, DvPSettlement (R62–66, R304–310). We chose three contracts. The name `AssetToken` matches the AI's proposal (R64). |
200	| Fixed sale price set at deployment (not issuer-set NAV) | Eliminates price oracle dependency; simplifies MVP | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI recommended issuer-set NAV and listed a fixed price as the simpler option (R265–267). |
201	| Instant subscription flow (not request-and-approve) | Reduces contract complexity; investor experience is clearer | AI proposed, human adopted (R270). |
202	| Escrow DvP in AssetSale (spec-v1 §4) | Sale contract holds inventory and proceeds | AI offered, human chose otherwise. The AI recommended approve-based DvP without escrow (R258–259). |
203	| Whitelist + pause + freeze + forced transfer as in-scope features | Directly addresses the "permissioning and compliance" requirement from v0 | AI proposed, human adopted. Freeze, forced transfer and pause were all rated "Must" (R296–297). D5 (3 November 2026) kept pause and forced transfer and dropped freeze, because whitelist revocation already does what freeze would. That narrowing was AI proposed, human adopted, in a Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) session. |
204	| Frontend split into three role-based dashboards | Matches the three-role model; each role sees only relevant actions | No AI proposal found. The AI suggested a different role split: Issuer, Compliance Agent, Investor (R310). |

1	# AssetToken: Tokenisation Using Blockchain
2

# AssetToken: Tokenisation Using Blockchain

An academic dApp for NTU SC4053. Authorised issuers tokenise fictional real-world and digital assets as ERC-20 tokens and sell them at a fixed price to whitelisted investors. All ownership records and compliance rules live on Ethereum. The repository is also graded on how the AI-written code was audited, so every change carries an evidence trail (see [Audit trail](#audit-trail)).

**Status (4 November 2026):** contracts, frontend and local tests are complete. Two things remain: a genuine MetaMask browser check ([AUD-002](docs/issues/AUD-002-frontend-dashboards-and-wallet-integration-are-uni.md)) and the public Sepolia deployment ([AUD-003](docs/issues/AUD-003-deployment-and-verification-tooling-are-incomplete.md)).

## What it does

| Contract | Role |
|---|---|
| `AssetFactory` | The platform admin authorises or revokes issuers. An authorised issuer creates an asset, which deploys an `AssetToken` and an `AssetSale` and records them in the registry (`getAsset`, `getAssetCount`). |
| `AssetToken` | A fixed-supply ERC-20 with 0 decimals. Every transfer requires a whitelisted sender and recipient. Revoking an investor keeps their balance but blocks sending, receiving and buying. The issuer can **pause** all token movement and **force-transfer** tokens out of a revoked address, for example to recover a lost key (decision D5). |
| `AssetSale` | Holds sale inventory and sells it at a fixed price, with exact ETH payment. The issuer withdraws proceeds, closes the sale and recovers unsold tokens. ETH forced in from outside can be swept. |

The frontend (React 18, Vite, ethers 6) has a marketplace, an investor portfolio with transfers, issuer and admin dashboards, and on-chain transaction history. The specification is [`docs/spec/spec-v1.md`](docs/spec/spec-v1.md). Where the later phase requirements in [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/) differ from it, those requirements and their recorded decisions (D1–D10) govern.

## Setup

Validated with Node 22.18.0 (Phase 4 session) and Node 24.15.0 with npm 11.12.1 on Windows. From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run compile
```

## Run locally

Use three terminals, all started in the repository root:

```bash
# Terminal 1: leave the local blockchain running
npm run node
```

```bash
# Terminal 2: deploy to that persistent chain and sync ABIs/configuration
npm run deploy:local

# Optional: seed CPT/DLT for exploration, only on an empty local registry
npm run demo:local
```

```bash
# Terminal 3: start the frontend
npm run dev --prefix frontend
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:5173**. You can browse without a wallet. To sign transactions, connect MetaMask and switch to **Local Ethereum**: chain **31337**, RPC **http://127.0.0.1:8545**, symbol **ETH**. The app offers to add this network when you ask to switch.

Use Hardhat local accounts 0–4 for the admin, the issuer, investor 1, investor 2 and an unapproved investor. Only import these development accounts into a separate development wallet or profile. Hardhat prints their publicly known keys in your terminal; never use them for real funds or commit them. The application never asks for, stores or reads wallet private keys or seed phrases.

Every deployment writes `frontend/src/config/addresses.json` and syncs the three compiled ABIs. After restarting or resetting the chain, deploy again and restart Vite. The app checks the deployment's block hash and runtime bytecode hash, not just its address. `npm run deploy:ephemeral` deploys to a throwaway in-process chain instead.

The UI has no pause or forced-transfer controls (spec-v1 §7 does not require them). The issuer calls them directly on the token contract. Forced transfers do appear in the transaction history.

## Tests

```bash
npm test                              # 132 contract tests
npm test --prefix frontend            # 113 frontend behaviour tests
npm run build --prefix frontend       # TypeScript + production Vite build
npx tsc --noEmit                      # root scripts and contract tests
npm run test:integration              # needs `npm run node` running; deploys its own fixture
bash scripts/evidence.sh <label>      # build, test, gas, coverage (slither if installed) into docs/evidence/runs/
```

The integration suite runs the production frontend services against real local contracts. It signs through an EIP-1193 adapter over Hardhat's unlocked accounts, so it does not test MetaMask. It covers the full lifecycle, including a forced transfer and a pause. The counts above are from 4 November 2026. Contract line coverage is 98.79%.

## Sepolia deployment

```bash
npm run deploy:sepolia
```

This builds with the optimised `production` profile (AUD-012). Every profile has the optimizer on (AUD-014): unoptimised, `AssetFactory` is right at the 24 576-byte EIP-170 limit, because it embeds the other two contracts. `hardhat.config.ts` reads `TESTNET_RPC_URL` and `PRIVATE_KEY` with `configVariable`, from environment variables or Hardhat's encrypted keystore (`npx hardhat keystore set PRIVATE_KEY`). Nothing loads a `.env` file automatically; [`.env.example`](.env.example) lists the names. Use a testnet burner wallet only.

## Audit trail

AI tools (Claude Code, Codex, claude.ai) generated the contracts, tests and frontend. Commit prefixes record who wrote each change. [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) sets the rules every AI session follows, including rules learned from each audit finding.

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| [`docs/issues/INDEX.md`](docs/issues/INDEX.md) | AUD-001 to AUD-014. AUD-001 to AUD-003 are tracking issues; the rest are defects. Each defect has before/after evidence and an analysis of why the AI made the mistake. Defects from AUD-005 onward, except AUD-009 and AUD-010 (Phase 4, uncommitted at the time), also have a separate failing-test commit and fix commit |
| [`docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`](docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md) | Every AI session: tool, model, context given and outcome. Transcripts are in `docs/ai-logs/raw/` (emails and Hardhat dev keys redacted, decisions D9 and D10) |
| Tags `ai-baseline-phase2`, `-phase3`, `-phase4`, `-d5` | Each first complete AI generation, never edited afterwards. The pre-AI spec is tagged `spec-v0` in the local repository but has not been pushed |
| [`docs/evidence/`](docs/evidence/) | Evidence runs and per-issue logs |
| [`docs/report/REPORT-MAP.md`](docs/report/REPORT-MAP.md) | Which evidence backs each section of the AI Audit Report |

Commit prefixes show who wrote what: `ai:`, `human:`, `test(AUD-NNN):`, `fix(AUD-NNN):`, `docs:`, `evidence:`, `chore:`. Implementation notes: [Phase 2](docs/phase2-implementation.md), [Phase 3](docs/phase3-implementation.md), [Phase 4](docs/phase4-implementation.md), [D5](docs/d5-implementation.md).

Academic demonstration only. Assets and token prices are simulated. Tokens do not represent legally enforceable ownership or investment claims.
